assets.name: Local BGA project source
assets.description: Game code, database definitions, and options inside a configured project root.

assets.name: Local files outside the project roots
assets.description: SSH keys, environment files, browser profiles, and unrelated repositories on the developer machine.

assets.name: BGA Studio credentials
assets.description: SSH keys, agent sockets, and session material that authenticate to BGA Studio.

assets.name: Remote Studio project
assets.description: Shared, hard-to-restore files, tables, and saved state belonging to a Studio project; the observed default readonly ACL can expose project source to other Studio developers.

assets.name: Player data
assets.description: Player identities and gameplay records reachable through Studio logs or tables.

assets.name: Release artifacts and verification evidence
assets.description: The published package, CI logs, coverage output, conformance output, and evidence files.

assets.name: MCP client context
assets.description: The agent context window and the actions an agent takes based on server output.

actors.name: BGA developer
actors.description: Runs the server, chooses its configuration, and owns the machine.

actors.name: MCP client or agent
actors.description: Sends tool arguments that may be model-generated, malformed, or unintended.

actors.name: Project file content
actors.description: File names, links, and text inside a project root, possibly authored by a third party.

actors.name: Documentation and community content
actors.description: Retrieved BGA Studio documentation, wiki pages, and community examples.

actors.name: BGA Studio service
actors.description: Remote SFTP and web endpoints whose responses the server would parse.

actors.name: Other BGA Studio developer
actors.description: A separate developer account that must not gain access to the dedicated private test project's source through the observed default readonly-sharing ACL.

actors.name: Dependency and CI supply chain
actors.description: npm packages, GitHub Actions, and the package manager used to build and publish.

trustBoundaries.name: MCP client to server
trustBoundaries.description: Tool arguments and resource URIs crossing into the server process.

trustBoundaries.name: Server to local filesystem
trustBoundaries.description: Every path the server resolves, opens, or lists on the developer machine.

trustBoundaries.name: Server process perimeter
trustBoundaries.description: Subprocess execution, environment access, and long-running work inside the server.

trustBoundaries.name: Server to client and artifacts
trustBoundaries.description: Tool results, errors, stderr logs, and retained CI evidence leaving the process. Every capability crosses it, whether or not it names it, so its open output surfaces apply to all of them.

trustBoundaries.name: Documentation retrieval
trustBoundaries.description: Outbound requests for documentation and the untrusted content they return. Reviewed 2026-08-07: a capability may cross only when every mitigation listed in preconditions is implemented.

trustBoundaries.name: BGA Studio synchronization
trustBoundaries.description: Authenticated SFTP and mutation traffic with a Studio project. Reviewed 2026-08-07: a capability may cross only when every precondition is implemented.

trustBoundaries.name: BGA Studio own-account reads
trustBoundaries.description: Authenticated reads of the developer's own Studio pages. Reviewed 2026-08-07 and reopened on the owner's decision: reading your own logs is reasonable, but the page is undocumented and the 2026-08-08 audit recorded additional planned controls in the boundary's abuse cases before release verification.

trustBoundaries.name: Build and release supply chain
trustBoundaries.description: Dependencies, CI actions, and published artifacts.

outputSurfaces.name: Successful MCP result
outputSurfaces.description: Text content and structured content of a tool or resource result that succeeded.

outputSurfaces.name: Published failure result
outputSurfaces.description: The message, code, and details of a refusal, a validation failure, or an unexpected error returned to the client.

outputSurfaces.name: Terminal diagnostics
outputSurfaces.description: What the command-line entry point prints for an operator, including the Studio preflight report.

outputSurfaces.name: Server log and launcher stderr
outputSurfaces.description: Every line the process writes to stderr, which an MCP launcher captures into its own log file.

outputSurfaces.name: Retained artifact
outputSurfaces.description: Verification evidence, packaged-run records, and anything else a CI job uploads or keeps.

abuseCases.title: Client requests a path outside a configured project root
abuseCases.impact: Private keys or unrelated source are read and copied into the client context.

abuseCases.title: A link inside a project root resolves outside it
abuseCases.impact: A crafted repository exfiltrates files the developer never configured.

abuseCases.title: Server is started without an explicit root and still answers project questions
abuseCases.impact: The server reads whatever the working directory happens to contain.

abuseCases.title: Tool arguments reach a shell, a URL, or a raw filesystem call
abuseCases.impact: Command or path injection executes code or reads arbitrary files.

abuseCases.title: A large or pathological project floods the client or hangs the server
abuseCases.impact: The agent context is swamped or the server stops responding to the client.

abuseCases.title: Secrets, absolute paths, or player data appear in a result or error
abuseCases.impact: Credentials or personal data are copied into an agent transcript that may be stored remotely.

abuseCases.title: Retained CI output carries a credential or private project data
abuseCases.impact: A public workflow artifact publishes a secret that must then be rotated.

abuseCases.title: Publisher artwork or private game code enters the repository through a fixture
abuseCases.impact: The project redistributes material it has no right to publish.

abuseCases.title: A Studio credential is passed as an ordinary tool argument
abuseCases.impact: The credential is logged in the client transcript and in server output.

abuseCases.title: A synchronization writes to the wrong Studio project
abuseCases.impact: Another developer's project is overwritten and cannot be restored.

abuseCases.title: A synchronization reuses a browser session or undocumented endpoint
abuseCases.impact: A future mutating adapter could expose session material or bypass the reviewed SFTP boundary.

abuseCases.title: Retrieved documentation contains instructions aimed at the agent
abuseCases.impact: The agent follows attacker text and takes actions the developer never requested.

abuseCases.title: A network capability sends local project source off the machine
abuseCases.impact: Unreleased game code leaves the developer machine without consent.

abuseCases.title: A dependency or CI action is replaced with a malicious version
abuseCases.impact: Arbitrary code runs on developer machines and in CI with repository access.

abuseCases.title: An agent executes a mutating operation the developer did not request
abuseCases.impact: Remote or local state changes without an explicit human decision.

abuseCases.title: A documentation fetch is aimed at an internal or loopback service
abuseCases.impact: The server becomes a proxy into the developer network, reaching services the client could not reach itself.

abuseCases.title: Project content leaves the machine inside a request
abuseCases.impact: A search built from file content sends unreleased game code to a third party in a URL or body.

abuseCases.title: A documentation response is slow or enormous
abuseCases.impact: The agent context is flooded or the server hangs waiting on a remote host.

abuseCases.title: Cached documentation is served as current
abuseCases.impact: A developer follows guidance that the framework has since changed, with nothing to reveal its age.

abuseCases.title: Outbound requests reveal what a developer is working on
abuseCases.impact: A third party learns which game and which problem a developer is working on, from timing and query terms alone.

abuseCases.title: A release claims verification the tests did not produce
abuseCases.impact: A capability is released as verified while a scenario proving it never ran, or the artifact saying so was edited afterwards.

abuseCases.title: A synchronization uploads files from outside the project
abuseCases.impact: Keys, environment files, or notes that never belonged to the game are copied to a third-party server.

abuseCases.title: Production Studio logs carry other players' identifiers into an agent's context
abuseCases.impact: Production error logs and Sentry issues name affected users, so reading them exports real players' data to wherever the agent's context goes. Logs from a developer's own Studio test tables are not this case: those identifiers are their own dev accounts.

abuseCases.title: A synchronization deletes or overwrites remote-only files
abuseCases.impact: SFTP has no version history, so a file that exists only on Studio is gone with no local copy to restore it from.

abuseCases.title: A private Studio test project exposes source through the default readonly-sharing ACL
abuseCases.impact: Unreleased project source can be visible to unrelated Studio developers even though the project was created as Private.

abuseCases.title: A file-sourced Studio session reaches a result, log line, or artifact
abuseCases.impact: The documented file provider can supply the live credential without registering that exact value for redaction.

abuseCases.title: A Studio credential or host reaches a result, a log line, or an artifact
abuseCases.impact: A credential that appears in stderr or a retained CI artifact must be rotated, and the developer may not know it leaked.

abuseCases.title: An authenticated Studio read connects to a non-public resolved address
abuseCases.impact: A valid alternate IP representation can bypass textual classification and reach a loopback or private address.

abuseCases.title: A Studio session source or response continues consuming resources after failure
abuseCases.impact: A special or oversized credential file, slow body, or ignored abort can hang or continue work after the public call returns.

mitigations.title: Only explicitly configured, existing project roots are accepted
Missing or invalid configuration denies the operation instead of guessing
Relative traversal, absolute paths, and null bytes are rejected lexically
Static paths are re-checked after the filesystem resolves links
Containment, type, and size checks are bound to the exact opened object and all encountered entries consume one budget
Current production source routes the enumerated filesystem, network, and subprocess imports through the policy boundary
Alternate specifiers, dynamic imports, re-exports, repository-owned wrappers, and privileged globals cannot bypass the policy boundary
The public caller receives a configured deadline failure when the timeout race expires
A deadline cancels and quiesces the underlying filesystem, parser, and network work before the operation settles
Successful tool results that reach the shared post-check are refused when their result payload exceeds the configured budget
Every final result payload, including failures, is bounded under a feasible configured minimum
A remote target must be allowlisted before any adapter may use it
Mutations are disabled by default and require an explicit confirmed target
Network access is off unless the developer enables it at startup
Shared failure publication redacts configured credentials, sessions, connection strings, player data, and outside paths
Successful text and structured results are minimized and redact exact configured secrets and known credential forms
Unexpected failures collapse to a stable code with no stack trace or internals
Server logs and stderr are redacted before they are written
Repository content is scanned for known credential formats
Retained CI artifacts, including the verification evidence, are scanned before upload and never contain the seeded secret
Fixtures may not contain publisher artwork, private source, or secrets
Every dependency is pinned exactly and installed from the frozen lockfile
Every GitHub Action is pinned to a full commit SHA
No network or mutating capability ships while its trust boundary is unreviewed
mitigations.cadence: Before advertising any capability or adapter that crosses an unreviewed boundary
mitigations.evidence: docs/THREAT_MODEL.md boundary table, enforced by pnpm verify:threat-model

mitigations.title: Client and agent trust expectations are documented for the developer
mitigations.evidence: SECURITY.md security expectations and docs/THREAT_MODEL.md operator responsibilities

mitigations.title: Studio credentials come from a dedicated provider, never from tool arguments
Browser sessions and undocumented endpoints stay unused pending a separate review
mitigations.cadence: Before any Studio log or table capability is implemented

mitigations.title: Documentation results carry source URL, snapshot date, and official or community provenance
Retrieved documentation is labelled as untrusted content and never as instructions
Only allowlisted documentation hosts over HTTPS, with redirects confined to the allowlist
Recognized dotted IPv4 and literal IPv6 loopback, link-local, and private forms are refused after resolution
Every resolved address is normalized semantically before non-public address classification and socket use
Documentation requests originate from the explicit tool argument and obvious pasted paths or known source markers are refused
The outbound-query contract makes consent or narrow semantics enforceable without claiming that string heuristics prove provenance
A successful documentation response body is read under an explicit byte budget and the public caller has a deadline
Timeouts, redirects, and non-success responses destroy or boundedly drain every body and socket before settlement
Cached documentation carries its snapshot date and is never served as current without one
Verification evidence records every advertised capability, and a scenario that did not run is recorded as missing
Verification evidence carries a digest of its own content, so an artifact edited after its run is detectable
The human threat model and the machine record agree field for field, and nothing is advertised as verified across an output surface only planned work covers
Studio credentials come from the environment or an agent, never from a tool argument
Only the documented Studio host and port over SFTP, with the host key verified against a stored fingerprint
A mutation names its exact remote project and the client repeats it back before anything is written
Only files inside the configured project root are uploaded, resolved through the policy that guards local reads
Every mutation has a dry run listing exactly what would change, and execution requires explicit intent
Deleting or overwriting a remote file with no local counterpart is refused rather than resolved
Credentials, hosts, and account names are redacted from every result, error, log line, and artifact
The dedicated private Studio project has cross-developer readonly source sharing disabled before live test data is seeded
mitigations.cadence: Before every live Studio test run until BGA-322 defines a repeatable supported check
mitigations.evidence: Live 2026-08-08 project inspection found the control enabled; BGA-322 blocks live testing

mitigations.title: Production logs and Sentry, test-table workflows, saved states, and player perspectives are not automated; experimental own-account Studio log reading is the reviewed exception
mitigations.cadence: Re-read if BGA publishes an API for production logs, tables, saved states, or perspectives
mitigations.evidence: docs/verification/STUDIO_BOUNDARY_REVIEW.md decision and the explicit BGA-312 own-account exception

mitigations.title: The Studio session is never accepted as a tool argument
Studio reads use one fixed Studio HTTPS host and path family and refuse redirects
The read_studio_logs MCP result withholds parsed lines not attributable to the developer's declared own accounts
Foreign and unattributable Studio values are absent from MCP content, setup output, CLI stdout and stderr, errors, and artifacts
Studio reads normalize every resolved address before non-public classification and socket use
Studio credential reads, requests, response bodies, and parsing stop and quiesce when the deadline expires
Successful Studio results minimize messages and redact exact configured secrets and known credential forms
An environment-sourced session value is removed from published errors, log lines, and artifacts
The server refuses the Studio file-session provider until it can establish a bounded regular protected file on the current platform
The exact normalized Studio session selected from a file provider is registered before any output is published
Production error logs and Sentry are never retrieved, because they are about real players

residualRisks.description: Packaged public-tool policy evidence now exists for selected refusal paths, but it does not prove final failure budgets, cancellation, a complete privileged-effect gate, or race-safe bounded traversal. BGA-325, BGA-326, BGA-329, and BGA-330 own those remaining gaps.

The Studio boundaries were reviewed on 2026-08-07. Synchronization remains unimplemented behind planned controls; experimental own-account log reading is discoverable but remains unreleased and has additional open correctness, privacy, address, cancellation, and credential-file controls from the 2026-08-08 audit.

Documentation retrieval is reviewed and implemented behind explicit network enablement, host restrictions, provenance, and untrusted-content labelling. Those controls do not prove arbitrary query provenance or prevent an agent from acting on hostile retrieved prose; BGA-324 and RR-DOC-INJECTION-RESIDUAL carry those limits.
The server cannot control what an agent does with a correct, redacted result. Operator judgement remains part of the safety model.
Secret scanning recognizes known credential formats. A novel or encoded secret can pass the gate, so redaction and the artifact allowlist remain the primary controls.

Labelling retrieved content as untrusted does not stop an agent from acting on it. No server-side control can; the mitigation reduces the chance an agent treats documentation as instruction, and the operator responsibilities carry the rest.

An allowlisted documentation host that is itself compromised serves attacker content over a trusted channel. Provenance and untrusted-content labelling limit the damage; the allowlist cannot prevent it.

SFTP has no version history. A previewed, confirmed synchronization that writes the intended file to the intended project can still overwrite something the developer wanted, and nothing on this side of the connection can undo it.
The documentation describes multiple developer accounts per person and says nothing about credential confidentiality. A credential the developer has already shared is outside this server's control.

The experimental log reader parses a Studio page BGA does not document or version. It can break without warning, and a page change could in principle alter what the privacy screen sees. The screen fails closed — an unreadable line is withheld — but the capability stays experimental and off by default for this reason.
